source.title: Revocable Learned State via Process Sidecars

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some equations and symbols are flattened or garbled, but the relevant experimental results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies gradient-ascent unlearning and RMU and reports targeted-secret extractability and refusal outcomes. It does not test whether attacks recover knowledge after successful unlearning.
record.gate_note: The paper’s process-sidecar results concern revoking memory while preserving later refusal behavior, not recovery through fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting. Robustness results from prior work are cited but not tested here. The unlearning-baseline results are retained; the main process-sidecar comparisons are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a memory-revocation paper, not a robustness study of unlearning. It runs RMU, NPO and gradient-ascent FT-unlearn as baselines on memorized canaries after an entity-tied safety phase. It reports, mostly in words, whether these methods bring secret distinguishability to chance. That bears only on the first part of version A, in a new setting. No recovery attack is run, so versions B–F are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly correct. More precisely, the authors conclude that process sidecars beat naive task arithmetic on refusal closure in every trial. Both leave secret distinguishability near chance (calibrated AUC ≈0.54). Gradient-ascent FT-unlearn forgets but collapses refusal, NPO degrades refusal mildly, and RMU changes little and fails to forget. They do not test recovery attacks.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates gradient-ascent FT-unlearning and an RMU baseline within a revocation-and-refusal-preservation setting; it does not implement or evaluate the claim’s recovery-attack recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Refusal outcomes vary by unlearning method and configuration; FT-unlearn refusal closure is strongly negative across the reported settings, while NPO is less damaging and RMU is near zero.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient-ascent FT-unlearn lowers secret extractability but drives entity-tied refusal closure far below the unedited checkpoint: −15 to −33 at 0.5B, −33 to −55 at 1.5B, −38.7 at 9B, and mean −146.8 on the structured canary.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: After a later safety phase, gradient-ascent unlearning of memorized facts destroys the refusal behavior learned around those facts.

fits_no_version.finding: NPO gives mildly negative refusal closure (mean −1.33). RMU leaves refusal closure near zero but also fails to forget.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning baselines trade off forgetting against refusal preservation differently in staged-training revocation.

record.problems: The study does not test the recovery attacks in the claim. RMU secret AUC is described qualitatively without a numerical value. Some FT-unlearn results are reported as ranges across configurations/trials, and the 9B FT-unlearn result is a single trial. The paper notes that its local safety-drift theory does not predict the magnitude of large refusal-collapse outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-specific attack, process-sidecar, or main-method comparison results were left out: the reported process-sidecar comparisons concern revocation and refusal closure, not recovery attacks. Other FT-unlearn grid details are summarized in the reported ranges in Table 4.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the canaries after unlearning is not tested. General-ability (skill-retention) outcomes are not reported for the FT-unlearn, NPO or RMU baselines. No numeric secret AUC is given for FT-unlearn or NPO.
No relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation and no analysis of blocking access versus deleting.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attack. The authors list adversarial extraction as open.
Process sidecars are not evaluated against any recovery attack.

missing.what: Secret-AUC positions of the FT-unlearn and NPO baselines, which are plotted but given no number in the text
Skill-retention (general-ability) outcomes for the FT-unlearn, NPO and RMU baselines

record.verdict_notes: The study's own method (process sidecars) is evaluated only on forgetting and refusal, not against attacks. It therefore gives no evidence for version F, and its own-method results are not rows. The calibrated-AUC metric flips anti-ranking, which is a mild adaptive evaluator but not an attack. The paper cites Hu et al. 2025 and Łucki et al. 2025 on recovery but does not test it.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test simple attacks after unlearning. It does not report whether attacks recover knowledge, and it does not report a general-ability outcome for the FT-unlearn baselines.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis that tests access-blocking versus deletion is reported.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
The process-sidecar method is not tested against the attacks in versions B–E.
